common_name: Variegated Greater Periwinkle (Vinca major with Cream-White Leaf Margins)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Variegata bears larger leaves edged in cream-white than plain Vinca major, and spreads vigorously, so site it where it can be contained.

directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, average soil, siting it where its vigorous spread can be contained by a bed edge, path, or other barrier, since Vinca major can naturalize aggressively in mild climates. Variegata bears larger, glossy leaves boldly edged in cream-white around a green center, brightening a shaded bank or slope more than the solid-green species, along with the same lavender-blue, pinwheel-shaped spring flowers typical of greater periwinkle. Its trailing stems root readily wherever they touch soil, making it effective for erosion control on shaded slopes, though its vigor means it needs monitoring near naturalized woodland areas. Cut back hard in late winter if growth becomes leggy or overgrown.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Ground Covers for Shade
University of Georgia Extension — Shade Ground Covers for the South

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Variegata bears classic cream-yellow striped leaf margins, one of the older and most widely available variegated liriope selections.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; liriope tolerates the full range of Gulf South conditions from clay to sandy soils and from moist to periodically drought-stressed. Variegata bears strap-shaped, dark green leaves edged in creamy yellow stripes, one of the classic, long-established variegated liriope selections that brightens border edges and mass plantings, topped in late summer by spikes of small lavender-purple flowers followed by black berries that persist into winter. As one of the most versatile groundcover plants for Gulf South landscapes, it works equally well as a border edge, foundation planting, or mass groundcover under trees. Divide established clumps every three to five years when they become overcrowded and flowering declines.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Ground Covers for Shade

common_name: Green Sheen Pachysandra (Extra-Glossy Compact Japanese Spurge)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown clumps in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Green Sheen bears unusually glossy, dark green leaves on a compact plant, holding better winter color than the species.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Japanese pachysandra spreads by underground rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing evergreen mat under trees and in shaded beds. Green Sheen bears notably glossy, lacquer-like dark green leaves on a more compact plant than the standard species, holding richer winter color and resisting the yellowing some pachysandra selections show in cold weather. Small white flower spikes appear at ground level in early spring, largely hidden beneath the foliage. It spreads steadily to form a uniform carpet over two to three years in suitable conditions, needing little maintenance beyond occasional edging to control spread.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Ground Covers for Shade
